claim: The bacterial outer membrane is a critical barrier that protects the cell from antibiotics and other environmental threats.
source: The bacterial outer membrane (OM) is a critical barrier that protects the cell from antibiotics and other environmental threats, and protects pathogenic bacteria from the anti-microbial responses of the host.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about bacterial outer membranes.

claim: The outer membrane protects pathogenic bacteria from the anti-microbial responses of the host.
source: The bacterial outer membrane (OM) is a critical barrier that protects the cell from antibiotics and other environmental threats, and protects pathogenic bacteria from the anti-microbial responses of the host.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about bacterial outer membranes.

claim: The outer membrane is an asymmetric bilayer, with an outer leaflet of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and a phospholipid inner leaflet.
source: The OM is an asymmetric bilayer, with an outer leaflet of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and a phospholipid inner leaflet.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about bacterial outer membrane structure.

claim: The outer membrane is separated from the inner membrane by the periplasmic space, which contains the peptidoglycan cell wall.
source: The OM is separated from the inner membrane (IM) by the periplasmic space, which contains the peptidoglycan cell wall.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about bacterial cell envelope structure.

claim: Energy from ATP and the proton motive force are associated with the cytoplasm and inner membrane, leaving the periplasm and outer membrane without direct access to these conventional energy sources.
source: Moreover, energy from ATP and the proton motive force are associated with the cytoplasm and inner membrane (IM), leaving the periplasm and OM without direct access to these conventional energy sources.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about energy sources in bacterial cells.

claim: Double-membraned bacteria have evolved protein machines to overcome the challenge of transporting molecules beyond the inner membrane.
source: Consequently, double-membraned bacteria have evolved a fascinating array of protein machines to overcome the challenge of transporting molecules beyond the IM.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about bacterial transport systems.

claim: The BAM complex is a passive catalyst for outer membrane protein insertion.
source: These include passive catalysts for OM protein insertion (BAM complex [Knowles et al., 2009; Gu et al., 2016; Han et al., 2016]), as well as ATP and proton-driven machines that couple energy from the cell interior to transport across the cell envelope.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on the BAM complex.

claim: The LPS transport system couples an inner membrane ABC transporter to a periplasmic bridge and outer membrane complex to export newly synthesized LPS from the inner membrane to the outer leaflet of the outer membrane.
source: An elegant example of this coupling is illustrated by the LPS transport system, which couples an IM ABC (ATP binding cassette) transporter to a periplasmic bridge and OM complex to export newly synthesized LPS from the IM to the outer leaflet of the OM (Okuda et al., 2012; Okuda et al., 2016; Sperandeo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on the LPS transport system.

claim: Comparatively little is known about how phospholipids are trafficked and inserted into the inner leaflet of the outer membrane.
source: In contrast to the trafficking and assembly of proteins and LPS in the OM, we know comparatively little about how phospholipids are trafficked and inserted into the inner leaflet of the OM, or how the asymmetry of the OM is maintained.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The Mla system is an ABC transporter in E. coli and related Gram-negative bacteria.
source: The Mla system, an ABC transporter in E. coli and related Gram-negative bacteria, has recently emerged as a key player in phospholipid transport across the bacterial envelope.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the Mla system.

claim: Mla trafficks phospholipids between the inner membrane and outer membrane.
source: Mla trafficks phospholipids between the IM and OM and is important for maintaining the outer membrane barrier (Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009; Chong et al., 2015; Thong et al., 2016; Abellón-Ruiz et al., 2017; Ekiert et al., 2017; Isom et al., 2017; Shrivastava et al., 2017; Powers and Trent, 2018; Yeow et al., 2018; Ercan et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2019; Kamischke et al., 2019; Shrivastava and Chng, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research on the Mla system.

claim: Mla is important for maintaining the outer membrane barrier.
source: Mla trafficks phospholipids between the IM and OM and is important for maintaining the outer membrane barrier (Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009; Chong et al., 2015; Thong et al., 2016; Abellón-Ruiz et al., 2017; Ekiert et al., 2017; Isom et al., 2017; Shrivastava et al., 2017; Powers and Trent, 2018; Yeow et al., 2018; Ercan et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2019; Kamischke et al., 2019; Shrivastava and Chng, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research on the Mla system.

claim: The Mla system consists of three main parts: an inner membrane ABC transporter complex (MlaFEDB), an outer membrane complex (MlaA-OmpC/F), and a soluble periplasmic protein (MlaC).
source: This system consists of three main parts: (1) an IM ABC transporter complex, MlaFEDB; (2) an OM complex, MlaA-OmpC/F; and (3) a soluble periplasmic protein, MlaC, which has been proposed to shuttle phospholipids between MlaFEDB and MlaA-OmpC/F (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the Mla system, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: MlaC has been proposed to shuttle phospholipids between MlaFEDB and MlaA-OmpC/F.
source: This system consists of three main parts: (1) an IM ABC transporter complex, MlaFEDB; (2) an OM complex, MlaA-OmpC/F; and (3) a soluble periplasmic protein, MlaC, which has been proposed to shuttle phospholipids between MlaFEDB and MlaA-OmpC/F (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statement about a proposed mechanism based on prior research.

claim: The directionality of transport facilitated by the Mla pathway is still an area of intense research.
source: The directionality of transport facilitated by the Mla pathway is still an area of intense research, with reports of both phospholipid import (Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009; Chong et al., 2015; Powers and Trent, 2018; Yeow et al., 2018) and export (Hughes et al., 2019; Kamischke et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations to conflicting research.

claim: There are reports of both phospholipid import and export by the Mla pathway.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research reporting both import and export.

evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the MlaFEDB complex, supported by citations.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of MlaFEDB was determined at 3.05 Å resolution.
source: To address how Mla drives lipid transport, we overexpressed the mla operon (Figure 1B), reconstituted the MlaFEDB ABC transporter complex in lipid nanodiscs containing E. coli polar lipids (see Materials and methods), and determined the structure using single-particle cryo-EM, with a nominal resolution of 3.05 Å (Figure 1C–E, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: MlaFEDB was reconstituted in lipid nanodiscs containing E. coli polar lipids.
source: To address how Mla drives lipid transport, we overexpressed the mla operon (Figure 1B), reconstituted the MlaFEDB ABC transporter complex in lipid nanodiscs containing E. coli polar lipids (see Materials and methods), and determined the structure using single-particle cryo-EM, with a nominal resolution of 3.05 Å (Figure 1C–E, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Initial reconstructions of MlaFEDB showed clear asymmetry.
source: Although MlaFEDB was expected to exhibit twofold symmetry, initial reconstructions showed clear asymmetry in our maps, which we then refined without applying symmetry (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The entire MlaFEDB complex is well-defined at ~2.8–3.5 Å resolution.
source: Local resolution analysis showed that the entire complex is well-defined at ~2.8–3.5 Å resolution (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), allowing us to build a nearly complete model for MlaFEDB (Figure 1F), including a high-resolution structure of the MlaE transmembrane subunit.
evidence: This is supported by the local resolution analysis of the cryo-EM map.

claim: A nearly complete model for MlaFEDB was built, including a high-resolution structure of the MlaE transmembrane subunit.
source: Local resolution analysis showed that the entire complex is well-defined at ~2.8–3.5 Å resolution (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), allowing us to build a nearly complete model for MlaFEDB (Figure 1F), including a high-resolution structure of the MlaE transmembrane subunit.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and model building described in the manuscript.

claim: Both coils of the membrane scaffold protein (MSP) belt surrounding the nanodisc were resolved.
source: In addition, we resolved both coils of the membrane scaffold protein (MSP) belt surrounding the nanodisc (Bayburt et al., 2002) using the map filtered at 6 Å, thereby clearly defining the position of the transmembrane domain (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The stoichiometry of MlaFEDB is MlaF2E2D6B2.
source: The MlaFEDB transporter is significantly larger and more complicated than most other structurally characterized ABC transporters, consisting of a total of 12 polypeptide chains from four different genes, with a stoichiometry of MlaF2E2D6B2.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and analysis.

claim: MlaFEDB consists of a total of 12 polypeptide chains from four different genes.
source: The MlaFEDB transporter is significantly larger and more complicated than most other structurally characterized ABC transporters, consisting of a total of 12 polypeptide chains from four different genes, with a stoichiometry of MlaF2E2D6B2.

source: At the center of the complex, a core ABC transporter module is formed from two copies each of the MlaF ATPase and the MlaE transmembrane domains (TMDs).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: A homohexameric ring of MCE domains from MlaD sits atop the periplasmic end of MlaE.
source: A homohexameric ring of MCE domains from MlaD sits atop the periplasmic end of MlaE like a crown.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The MCE ring is anchored in place by six MlaD transmembrane helices, which dock around the periphery of the MlaE TMDs.
source: This MCE ring is anchored in place by six MlaD transmembrane helices, which dock around the periphery of the MlaE TMDs (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Each of the MlaF ATPase subunits is bound to MlaB on the cytoplasmic side.
source: On the cytoplasmic side, each of the MlaF ATPase subunits is bound to MlaB, a STAS domain protein that was recently reported to act as regulator of the MlaFEDB transporter (Kolich et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and a citation to prior research.

claim: MlaB was recently reported to act as a regulator of the MlaFEDB transporter.
source: On the cytoplasmic side, each of the MlaF ATPase subunits is bound to MlaB, a STAS domain protein that was recently reported to act as regulator of the MlaFEDB transporter (Kolich et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The overall structure of the MlaF2B2 module is very similar to the recent MlaFB X-ray structure (PDB: 6XGY).
source: The overall structure of the MlaF2B2 module is very similar to our recent MlaFB X-ray structure (PDB: 6XGY), apart from a small relative rotation between the MlaF helical and catalytic subdomains (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the cryo-EM structure to a prior X-ray structure.

claim: There is a small relative rotation between the MlaF helical and catalytic subdomains compared to the X-ray structure.
source: The overall structure of the MlaF2B2 module is very similar to our recent MlaFB X-ray structure (PDB: 6XGY), apart from a small relative rotation between the MlaF helical and catalytic subdomains (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the cryo-EM structure to a prior X-ray structure.

claim: The rotation between MlaF subdomains is similar to motions described in other ABC transporters.
source: This rotation is similar to motions described in other ABC transporters (Karpowich et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2002; Orelle et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on ABC transporters.

claim: An unusual C-terminal extension of each MlaF protomer wraps around the neighboring MlaF subunit and docks near the MlaFB interface.
source: An unusual C-terminal extension of each MlaF protomer wraps around the neighboring MlaF subunit and docks near the MlaFB interface, almost identical to the domain-swapped 'handshake' motif observed in the crystal structure of the MlaF2B2 subcomplex (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B; Kolich et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and comparison to a prior X-ray structure.

claim: The MlaFEB subcomplex exhibits near-perfect twofold rotational symmetry at this resolution.
source: While the MlaFEB subcomplex exhibits near-perfect twofold rotational symmetry at this resolution, the MlaD ring is clearly tilted relative to MlaE, resulting in a misalignment of the twofold symmetry axis of MlaFEB and the pseudo-sixfold axis of MlaD by approximately 6° (Figure 1F).

claim: The MlaD ring is clearly tilted relative to MlaE.

evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and analysis.

claim: The twofold symmetry axis of MlaFEB and the pseudo-sixfold axis of MlaD are misaligned by approximately 6°.
source: While the MlaFEB subcomplex exhibits near-perfect twofold rotational symmetry at this resolution, the MlaD ring is clearly tilted relative to MlaE, resulting in a misalignment of the twofold symmetry axis of MlaFEB and the pseudo-sixfold axis of MlaD by approximately 6° (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and analysis.

source: Our cryo-EM structure reveals that the core TMD of MlaE consists of five transmembrane helices (TM1 - TM5) (Figure 2A and E–G).

source: Two additional N-terminal helices are membrane embedded, which we call interfacial helices 1 and 2 (IF1 and IF2 [Chen et al., 2020]; discussed in more detail below).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

source: The IF1 helix is a 30-residue long, amphipathic N-terminal helix that lies parallel to the membrane within the cytoplasmic leaflet, and extends along the width of the MlaE dimer (Figures 2A and 3B).

source: Although the C-terminal portion of IF1 interacts with TM3 and TM4, the N-terminal half projects outward into the surrounding membrane, creating a cleft between the core TMD and the IF1 helix (Figure 3A,B).

claim: The N-terminal half of IF1 projects outward into the surrounding membrane, creating a cleft between the core TMD and the IF1 helix.
source: Although the C-terminal portion of IF1 interacts with TM3 and TM4, the N-terminal half projects outward into the surrounding membrane, creating a cleft between the core TMD and the IF1 helix (Figure 3A,B).

source: Despite negligible sequence similarity, the core MlaE fold is related to the TMDs of several other ABC transporters.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: MlaE most closely resembles the LPS exporter LptF/LptG and the macrolide antibiotic efflux pump MacB.
source: MlaE most closely resembles the LPS exporter LptF/LptG (Thomas et al., 2020) and the macrolide antibiotic efflux pump MacB (Crow et al., 2017; Fitzpatrick et al., 2017; Okada et al., 2017; Figure 2B–J), but also shares similarities with the glycolipid flippases Wzm (Bi et al., 2018; Caffalette et al., 2019) and TarG (Chen et al., 2020) and the eukaryotic ABCA/ABCG families (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: MlaE shares similarities with the glycolipid flippases Wzm and TarG and the eukaryotic ABCA/ABCG families.

evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

source: Second, in both MlaE and LptFG, TM5 exists as one continuous helix, whereas TarG, Wzm, and ABCA/ABCG have a small insertion near the periplasmic end that results in a pair of reentrant helices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

source: Second, in both MlaE and LptFG, TM5 exists as one continuous helix, whereas TarG, Wzm, and ABCA/ABCG have a small insertion near the periplasmic end that results in a pair of reentrant helices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

In MacB, TarG, Wzm, and ABCA/ABCG transporters, IF2 forms an amphipathic helix that runs roughly parallel to the membrane within the cytoplasmic leaflet, followed by a sharp turn and a separate TM1, which spans nearly the entire bilayer (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).

source: In contrast, LptFG has no clear IF2 counterpart, as these TMDs begin with TM1 forming a long, continuous helix (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).

source: First, the MlaE core TMDs interact with two of the MlaD TM helices; second, the IF1 helices of the MlaE dimer interact with the remaining four MlaD TM helices; and third, the periplasmic end of the MlaE dimer interacts with the MlaD ring.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The periplasmic end of the MlaE dimer interacts with the MlaD ring.
source: First, the MlaE core TMDs interact with two of the MlaD TM helices; second, the IF1 helices of the MlaE dimer interact with the remaining four MlaD TM helices; and third, the periplasmic end of the MlaE dimer interacts with the MlaD ring.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The six identical transmembrane helices of MlaD interact with MlaE in three non-equivalent ways due to the symmetry mismatch.
source: Due to the symmetry mismatch between the pseudo-sixfold symmetric MlaD hexamer and the two-fold symmetric MlaFEB module, the six identical transmembrane helices of MlaD interact with MlaE in three non-equivalent ways (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and analysis.

claim: The MlaD TMs from chains A and D (MlaD-TMA/D) are closely packed against the MlaE TMDs on opposite sides of the complex.
source: The MlaD TMs from chains A and D (MlaD-TMA/D) are closely packed against the MlaE TMDs on opposite sides of the complex.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The remaining four TM helices from MlaD are largely isolated in the membrane, and their main interactions are with the MlaE IF1 helices via helix crossing interactions.
source: The remaining four TM helices from MlaD are largely isolated in the membrane, and their main interactions are with the MlaE IF1 helices via helix crossing interactions, with MlaD-TMB/E and MlaD-TMC/F contacting IF1 residues 6–14 and 17–25, respectively (~84° crossing angle, Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and analysis.

claim: The residues of IF1 interacting with the MlaD-TMB/E and MlaD-TMC/F helices form two well-conserved LxxF/LG motifs.
source: The residues of IF1 interacting with the MlaD-TMB/E and MlaD-TMC/F helices form two well-conserved LxxF/LG motifs, with the conserved Gly11 of each MlaD TM making close packing interactions with the two conserved Gly residues from IF1 (Gly10 and Gly21).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and sequence analysis.

claim: MlaD chimeras in which the native TM helix was replaced with a TM helix from LptC or LetB were unable to restore growth of an mlaD knockout strain in the presence of SDS+EDTA.
source: We found that neither of the MlaD chimeras were able to restore growth of an mlaD knockout strain in the presence of SDS+EDTA (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the genetic complementation assay data.

claim: MlaD chimeras with TM helices from LptC or LetB did not co-purify with MlaE, MlaB, and MlaF.
source: SDS-PAGE showed that MlaE co-purified with MlaB, MlaF and WT MlaD, but MlaD chimeras did not co-purify (Figure 3D), despite robust expression of hexameric MlaD in the membrane fraction (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the SDS-PAGE and purification data.

claim: The MlaD TM helix interactions with MlaE drive specificity in the formation of the complex.
source: These results suggest that the MlaD TM helix interactions with MlaE drive specificity in the formation of the complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic complementation and purification data.

claim: Single mutations in MlaD predicted to interfere with the interactions between MlaE and MlaD-TMA/D had no effect on the complementation of an mlaD knockout strain.
source: Single mutations in MlaD predicted to interfere with the interactions between MlaE and MlaD-TMA/D by creating steric clashes (Ala17Phe, Ala20Phe, or Val24Phe) or removing a bulky hydrophobic residue (Phe13Ala) had no effect on the complementation of an mlaD knockout strain (Figure 3A,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the genetic complementation assay data.

claim: A triple mutant of MlaD (Ala17Phe/Ala20Phe/Val24Phe) failed to complement an mlaD knockout strain, but yielded intact MlaFEDB complexes when overexpressed and purified.
source: In contrast, a triple mutant (Ala17Phe/Ala20Phe/Val24Phe) failed to complement, but yielded intact MlaFEDB complexes when overexpressed and purified (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by the genetic complementation assay and purification data.

claim: The interactions made by the MlaD-TMA/D helices may be redundant for MlaFEDB complex assembly because the remaining MlaD-TMB/E and MlaD-TMC/F helices can compensate.
source: These results indicate that the interactions made by the MlaD-TMA/D helices may be redundant for MlaFEDB complex assembly because the remaining MlaD-TMB/E and MlaD-TMC/F helices can compensate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic complementation and purification data.

claim: The interactions made by the MlaD-TMA/D helices are required for transporter function in cells.
source: However, the interactions made by the MlaD-TMA/D helices are required for transporter function in cells, suggesting a possible role in mechanism, such as modulating conformational change.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic complementation data.

claim: MlaE truncation mutants with 15 or 25 residues deleted from the N-terminus of IF1 fully restored growth of an mlaE knockout under SDS+EDTA conditions.
source: We observed that both the Δ1–15 aa and Δ1–25 aa mutants fully restored growth of an mlaE knockout under these conditions, similar to complementation by the WT operon (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the genetic complementation assay data.

claim: Point mutations in MlaD at positions predicted to disrupt interactions with both conserved LxxF/LG motifs in IF1 were able to fully complement an mlaD knockout.
source: Consistent with these results, when point mutations were introduced into MlaD at positions predicted to disrupt interactions with both conserved LxxF/LG motifs in IF1, all mutants tested were able to fully complement an mlaD knockout (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by the genetic complementation assay data.

claim: All the MlaE truncation mutants expressed well and formed complexes with MlaD, MlaF, and MlaB.
source: All the MlaE truncation mutants expressed well, and formed complexes with MlaD, MlaF, and MlaB (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C), although we noted that all the mutants appeared to incorporate less MlaFB into the complex.
evidence: This is supported by the purification data.

claim: The interactions between the IF1 helix of MlaE and the MlaD-TMB/E / MlaD-TMC/F helices are not strictly required, but likely contribute to MlaFEDB complex stability.
source: Thus, while the interactions between the IF1 helix of MlaE and the MlaD-TMB/E / MlaD-TMC/F helices are not strictly required, they likely still contribute to MlaFEDB complex stability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic complementation and purification data.

claim: MlaE mutants with larger deletions of IF1 (Δ1–30 aa) only partially restored growth, or failed to complement (Δ1–39 aa).
source: Finally, while the region of IF1 that interacts with MlaD appears to be dispensable, MlaE mutants with larger deletions only partially restored growth (Δ1–30 aa), or failed to complement (Δ1–39 aa), suggesting that the C-terminus of IF1 and/or the following loop has an essential function (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by the genetic complementation assay data.

claim: The C-terminus of IF1 and/or the following loop has an essential function.
source: Finally, while the region of IF1 that interacts with MlaD appears to be dispensable, MlaE mutants with larger deletions only partially restored growth (Δ1–30 aa), or failed to complement (Δ1–39 aa), suggesting that the C-terminus of IF1 and/or the following loop has an essential function (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic complementation assay data.

claim: The structure of MlaE is in the outward-open state.
source: While the vast majority of ABC transporter structures adopt an inward-open conformation in the absence of nucleotide (Gerber et al., 2008; Kadaba et al., 2008; Aller et al., 2009; Manolaridis et al., 2018), our structure of MlaE is in the outward-open state (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and comparison to other ABC transporters.

claim: The outward-open conformation was previously observed in the related transporters LptFG and MacB.
source: This uncommon configuration was previously observed in the related transporters LptFG (Li et al., 2019; Owens et al., 2019) and MacB (Fitzpatrick et al., 2017), suggesting that Mla, Lpt, and MacAB may share some mechanistic features.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: Mla, Lpt, and MacAB may share some mechanistic features.
source: This uncommon configuration was previously observed in the related transporters LptFG (Li et al., 2019; Owens et al., 2019) and MacB (Fitzpatrick et al., 2017), suggesting that Mla, Lpt, and MacAB may share some mechanistic features.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural similarity.

claim: The narrow outward-open pocket within MlaE encloses a volume of ~750 Å3.
source: The narrow outward-open pocket within MlaE encloses a volume of ~750 Å3 (estimated using CASTp [Tian et al., 2018]) and is primarily formed by TM1 and TM2, with some contribution from TM5 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and volume calculation.

claim: The outward-open pocket in MlaE is primarily formed by TM1 and TM2, with some contribution from TM5.
source: The narrow outward-open pocket within MlaE encloses a volume of ~750 Å3 (estimated using CASTp [Tian et al., 2018]) and is primarily formed by TM1 and TM2, with some contribution from TM5 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The pocket in LptFG has a volume of ~3000 Å3.
source: This is similar to LptFG, where TM1, TM2, and TM5 form a much larger pocket (volume of ~3000 Å3, estimated using CASTp [Tian et al., 2018], PDB: 6MHU [Li et al., 2019]) at the periplasmic side of the complex for LPS binding.
evidence: This is supported by volume calculation using a prior structure.

claim: The pockets in both MlaE and LptFG are largely hydrophobic in nature, consistent with binding to lipid substrates.
source: The pockets in both transporters are largely hydrophobic in nature, consistent with binding to lipid substrates, although in LptFG the rim has a pronounced positive charge proposed to interact with phosphates on the LPS inner core (Li et al., 2019), while MlaE is more neutral.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and comparison to LptFG.

claim: In LptFG the rim of the pocket has a pronounced positive charge proposed to interact with phosphates on the LPS inner core.
source: The pockets in both transporters are largely hydrophobic in nature, consistent with binding to lipid substrates, although in LptFG the rim has a pronounced positive charge proposed to interact with phosphates on the LPS inner core (Li et al., 2019), while MlaE is more neutral.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research on LptFG.

claim: The pore of MlaD and the outward-open pocket of MlaE line up with each other, resulting in a continuous hydrophobic pathway.
source: Indeed, in our structure of the MlaFEDB complex, the pore of MlaD and the outward-open pocket of MlaE line up with each other, resulting in a continuous hydrophobic pathway that runs from the pocket of MlaE, through MlaD, and out into the periplasm (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Additional density was apparent in the outward-open pocket of MlaE, which is the right size and shape to accommodate two diacyl phospholipids.
source: Additional density was apparent in the outward-open pocket of MlaE, which is the right size and shape to accommodate two diacyl phospholipids (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data.

claim: Two phosphatidylethanolamine molecules were modeled in the outward-open pocket of MlaE.
source: We modeled these as the most abundant PL species in E. coli, phosphatidylethanolamine, and these lipids make extensive contacts with both MlaE subunits, as well as MlaD (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A; see Materials and methods for additional details).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and modeling.

claim: The lipids bound to MlaFEDB appear to be trapped in different conformations.
source: Unlike recent structures of the LPS exporter bound to LPS, where all of the acyl chains project downward into the hydrophobic pocket of LptFG (Li et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2019), the lipids bound to MlaFEDB appear to be trapped in different conformations (Figure 4C), perhaps intermediates in the process of being transferred between MlaE and the MlaD pore.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and comparison to LptFG.

claim: In lipid 1, both acyl chains are bound in the pocket of MlaE.
source: In one lipid molecule (lipid 1), both acyl chains are bound in the pocket of MlaE (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and modeling.

claim: Lipid 2 adopts an extended conformation, with one acyl chain reaching down into the MlaE pocket, while the other projects upwards to insert into a constriction in the MlaD pore.
source: Strikingly, the second lipid (lipid 2) adopts an extended conformation, with one acyl chain reaching down into the MlaE pocket, while the other projects upwards to insert into a constriction in the MlaD pore formed by Leu106 and Leu107 (Figure 4D), which have previously been implicated in MlaD function (Ekiert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and modeling.

claim: The upward-facing acyl chain of lipid 2 is sandwiched between two tyrosine residues (Tyr81 from each MlaE subunit).
source: The upward-facing acyl chain of lipid 2 is sandwiched between two tyrosine residues (Tyr81 from each MlaE subunit), and these residues also contact one of the acyl chains of lipid 1.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and modeling.

claim: Mutations of Tyr81 to either Ala or Trp had no effect on E. coli growth in the presence of SDS+EDTA.
source: Mutations of Tyr81 to either a smaller (Ala) or a larger (Trp) hydrophobic residue had no effect on E. coli growth in the presence of SDS+EDTA (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), although a Tyr81Glu mutation was recently reported to impair MlaFEDB function (Tang, 2020) (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by the genetic complementation assay data.

claim: A Tyr81Glu mutation was recently reported to impair MlaFEDB function.
source: Mutations of Tyr81 to either a smaller (Ala) or a larger (Trp) hydrophobic residue had no effect on E. coli growth in the presence of SDS+EDTA (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), although a Tyr81Glu mutation was recently reported to impair MlaFEDB function (Tang, 2020) (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The polar head group of each lipid projects outwards through lateral solvent accessible channels on opposite sides of the complex.
source: In contrast to the hydrophobic fatty acid tails, which are completely buried within the MlaE-MlaD tunnel, the polar head group of each lipid projects outwards through lateral solvent accessible channels on opposite sides of the complex.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and modeling.

claim: The density for the lipid head groups in the lateral channels of MlaFEDB are not well resolved beyond the phosphoglycerol core.
source: Beyond the phosphoglycerol core, the density for the lipid head groups in the lateral channels of MlaFEDB are not well resolved, and the only noteworthy interaction is a salt bridge formed between Arg97 of MlaE and the head group phosphate (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data.

claim: A salt bridge is formed between Arg97 of MlaE and the head group phosphate.
source: Beyond the phosphoglycerol core, the density for the lipid head groups in the lateral channels of MlaFEDB are not well resolved, and the only noteworthy interaction is a salt bridge formed between Arg97 of MlaE and the head group phosphate (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and modeling.

claim: Weaker density beyond the phosphate may reflect heterogeneity in the lipid species bound to MlaFEDB in the structure.
source: Weaker density beyond the phosphate may reflect heterogeneity in the lipid species bound to MlaFEDB in our structure, and/or that the interactions between the headgroup and nearby MlaE and MlaD residues may be weak and non-specific.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the cryo-EM data.

claim: The crystal structure of MlaC bound to phospholipid revealed a similar binding mode and lack of head group specificity.
source: The crystal structure of MlaC bound to phospholipid revealed a similar binding mode and lack of head group specificity (Ekiert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The lateral channels may serve as a non-specific cavity to accommodate a range of polar head groups during lipid translocation.
source: Thus, rather than mediate the binding of specific lipids, the lateral channels may instead serve as a non-specific cavity to accommodate a range of polar head groups during the 'lipid gymnastics' (Neumann et al., 2017) that may need to occur to translocate lipids between the MlaE pocket and the MlaD pore, which likely involve flipping the lipids upside down (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the cryo-EM data and prior research.

claim: Arg97 is part of a cluster of conserved charged residues, including Glu98, Lys205, and Asp250, which form salt bridges buried in the hydrophobic core of MlaE.
source: In addition to interactions with the lipid head groups, Arg97 is part of a cluster of conserved charged residues, including Glu98, Lys205, and Asp250, which form salt bridges buried in the hydrophobic core of MlaE and are part of a larger polar interaction network including Gln73, Asp198, and Thr254 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and sequence analysis.

claim: Mutations of Arg97, Glu98, Lys205, and Asp250 individually to alanine had no effect on E. coli growth in the presence of SDS+EDTA.
source: To probe the potential role of these residues in MlaFEDB function, we mutated Arg97, Glu98, Lys205, and Asp250 individually to alanine, and found that these mutations had no effect on E. coli growth in the presence of SDS+EDTA (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by the genetic complementation assay data.

claim: The presence of two lipid densities in the structure raises the possibility that the Mla system may transport two substrates per transport cycle.
source: The presence of two lipid densities in our structure raises the possibility that the Mla system may transport two substrates per transport cycle.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the cryo-EM data.

claim: Structures of MlaC have been determined with either one or two diacyl phospholipids bound.
source: Structures of the periplasmic lipid carrier protein, MlaC, have been determined with either one or two diacyl phospholipids bound (Ekiert et al., 2017; Figure 4—figure supplement 4), and a structure of apo E. coli MlaC revealed a clamshell-like motion resulting in significant changes in the volume of the lipid binding pocket (Hughes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: A structure of apo E. coli MlaC revealed a clamshell-like motion resulting in significant changes in the volume of the lipid binding pocket.
source: Structures of the periplasmic lipid carrier protein, MlaC, have been determined with either one or two diacyl phospholipids bound (Ekiert et al., 2017; Figure 4—figure supplement 4), and a structure of apo E. coli MlaC revealed a clamshell-like motion resulting in significant changes in the volume of the lipid binding pocket (Hughes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The different architectures and conformational states of the MlaC pocket suggest that it may accommodate one or two phospholipids, or larger lipid molecules.
source: The different architectures and conformational states of the MlaC pocket suggest that it may accommodate one or two phospholipids, or larger lipid molecules.
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior structural studies.

claim: Previous studies have suggested that cardiolipin may be a substrate of the Mla system.
source: Indeed, previous studies have suggested that cardiolipin may be a substrate of the Mla system (Kamischke et al., 2019), and cardiolipin is detected by TLC in lipid extracts from components of the Mla system (Hughes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cardiolipin is detected by TLC in lipid extracts from components of the Mla system.
source: Indeed, previous studies have suggested that cardiolipin may be a substrate of the Mla system (Kamischke et al., 2019), and cardiolipin is detected by TLC in lipid extracts from components of the Mla system (Hughes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The presence of two phospholipids/four acyl chains bound in the MlaFEDB structure raises the possibility that the Mla system may be capable of transporting tetra-acyl lipids, such as cardiolipin.
source: Together with previous functional data, the presence of two phospholipids/four acyl chains bound in our MlaFEDB structure raises the possibility that the Mla system may also be capable of transporting tetra-acyl lipids, such as cardiolipin.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the cryo-EM data and prior research.

claim: The MlaD ring is tilted with respect to MlaFEB by approximately 6°.
source: Viewed from the side, the MlaD ring is tilted with respect to MlaFEB by approximately 6° (Figure 1F) and deviates from the expected sixfold symmetry observed in the crystal structure of MlaD and other MCE proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and comparison to prior structures.

claim: The MlaD ring deviates from the expected sixfold symmetry observed in the crystal structure of MlaD and other MCE proteins.
source: Viewed from the side, the MlaD ring is tilted with respect to MlaFEB by approximately 6° (Figure 1F) and deviates from the expected sixfold symmetry observed in the crystal structure of MlaD and other MCE proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and comparison to prior structures.

claim: Differences between MlaD subunits that result in symmetry breaking include re-organization of two of the six pore lining loops as well as domain level rearrangements in the ring.
source: Differences between subunits that result in symmetry breaking include re-organization of two of the six pore lining loops (containing Leu107) as well as domain level rearrangements in the ring (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and comparison to prior structures.

claim: The asymmetry of the MlaD ring appears to arise from its asymmetric interactions with lipid 1 at the interface of MlaE and MlaD.
source: Thus, the asymmetry in MlaD appears to arise from its asymmetric interactions with lipid 1 at the interface of MlaE and MlaD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Leu107 from MlaD chain F makes hydrophobic interactions with one of the fatty acid tails of lipid 1.
source: Leu107 from MlaD chain F makes hydrophobic interactions with one of the fatty acid tails, perhaps stabilizing this side of the MlaD ring in closer proximity to MlaE and the lipid-binding pocket.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The conformational changes in the MlaD ring could be important for lipid translocation through the channel or modulating the binding of MlaC to the transporter.
source: The resulting conformational changes in the MlaD ring could be important for lipid translocation through the channel or perhaps even modulating the binding of MlaC to the transporter and facilitating lipid transfer between MlaD and MlaC (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Site-specific photocross-linking was used to detect binding of radiolabeled phospholipids in vivo.
source: To assess whether phospholipids are bound in the pocket of MlaE in cells, we utilized a site-specific photocross-linking method (Isom et al., 2020) to detect binding of radiolabeled phospholipids in vivo.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: The unnatural photocross-linking amino acid p-benzoyl-L-phenylalanine (BPA) was incorporated into MlaE at five positions in the lipid-binding site.
source: We incorporated the unnatural photocross-linking amino acid p-benzoyl-L-phenylalanine (BPA) (Chin et al., 2002) into the MlaE protein at five positions in the lipid-binding site (Leu70, Val77, Leu78, Tyr81, and Leu99), as well as Phe209 (protected in the MlaE core; not expected to contact lipids) or Trp149 (membrane exposed; expected to contact bulk membrane lipids) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Both a monomeric and dimeric form of MlaE were observed, the latter of which was enriched in cross-linked samples where BPA had been incorporated at the dimer interface.
source: We observed both a monomeric and dimeric form of MlaE, the latter of which was enriched in cross-linked samples where BPA had been incorporated at the dimer interface (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the cross-linking data.

claim: Cross-linking at Trp149 resulted in high 32P signal, indicative of an abundance of phospholipids near the membrane-exposed Trp149.
source: Cross-linking at Trp149 and Phe209 resulted in high and low 32P signal, respectively, indicative of an abundance of phospholipids near the membrane-exposed Trp149 and very few phospholipids near the buried Phe209, as expected (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the cross-linking data.

claim: Cross-linking at Phe209 resulted in low 32P signal, indicative of very few phospholipids near the buried Phe209.
source: Cross-linking at Trp149 and Phe209 resulted in high and low 32P signal, respectively, indicative of an abundance of phospholipids near the membrane-exposed Trp149 and very few phospholipids near the buried Phe209, as expected (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the cross-linking data.

claim: 32P incorporation into MlaE was induced by cross-linkers at all five positions in the outward-open lipid binding pocket.
source: 32P incorporation into MlaE was induced by cross-linkers at all five positions in the outward-open lipid binding pocket, with particularly high signals for Tyr81 and Leu99 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the cross-linking data.

claim: The uncross-linked controls showed a weak signal, indicating that the elevated 32P signal in the cross-linked samples was due to the formation of cross-links between BPA and phospholipids.
source: Furthermore, the uncross-linked controls showed a weak signal, indicating that the elevated 32P signal in the cross-linked samples was due to the formation of cross-links between BPA and phospholipids at those locations.
evidence: This is supported by the cross-linking data.

claim: The phospholipid-binding site observed in the MlaFEDB structure is occupied by phospholipids in vivo.
source: Thus, the phospholipid-binding site observed in our MlaFEDB structure is occupied by phospholipids in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by the cross-linking data.

claim: MlaE is structurally related to two bacterial exporters (LPS exporter and MacAB).
source: The results presented here provide mechanistic insights into lipid transport by the Mla system. Our structure reveals that MlaE is structurally related to two bacterial exporters (LPS exporter and MacAB).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and structural comparison.

claim: A role for MlaFEDB in phospholipid export is supported by recent cellular studies in Acinetobacter baumannii.
source: A role for MlaFEDB in phospholipid export is supported by recent cellular studies in Acinetobacter baumannii (Kamischke et al., 2019), as well as in vitro experiments with E. coli proteins, showing directional lipid transfer from MlaD to MlaC (Ercan et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In vitro experiments with E. coli proteins show directional lipid transfer from MlaD to MlaC.
source: A role for MlaFEDB in phospholipid export is supported by recent cellular studies in Acinetobacter baumannii (Kamischke et al., 2019), as well as in vitro experiments with E. coli proteins, showing directional lipid transfer from MlaD to MlaC (Ercan et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Prior studies indicated that the Mla system is an importer.
source: On the other hand, prior studies indicated that the Mla system is an importer (Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009; Chong et al., 2015; Powers and Trent, 2018; Yeow et al., 2018), and in vitro reconstitution and transport assays suggest that MlaFEDB may be bi-directional, with a preference for import (retrograde transport) (Tang, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In vitro reconstitution and transport assays suggest that MlaFEDB may be bi-directional, with a preference for import (retrograde transport).
source: On the other hand, prior studies indicated that the Mla system is an importer (Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009; Chong et al., 2015; Powers and Trent, 2018; Yeow et al., 2018), and in vitro reconstitution and transport assays suggest that MlaFEDB may be bi-directional, with a preference for import (retrograde transport) (Tang, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Two other groups also reported structures of the MlaFEDB complex on BioRxiv concurrently with this preprint.
source: Concurrently with our preprint, two other groups also reported structures of the MlaFEDB complex on BioRxiv (Coudray, 2020; Mann, 2020; Tang, 2020), and these structures appear to be similar overall, although the PDB coordinates are not yet available to analyze.
evidence: This is a statement about concurrent research.

claim: An additional group published structures of MlaFEDB while this manuscript was under review.
source: While this manuscript was under review, an additional group also published structures of MlaFEDB (Chi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about concurrent research.

claim: In the lipid export model, phospholipids must be extracted from the inner membrane and reach the outward-open pocket of MlaE.
source: In anterograde phospholipid export (Figure 6A), first, phospholipids must be extracted from the inner membrane and reach the outward-open pocket of MlaE, from either the inner or outer leaflet (Hughes, 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of lipid export.

claim: It is plausible that MlaFEDB may extract phospholipids from the outer leaflet of the inner membrane.
source: Due to the structural similarities between MlaE and LptFG, which extracts LPS from the outer leaflet, it is plausible that MlaFEDB may extract PLs from the outer leaflet as well.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural similarity.

claim: It is possible that MlaFEDB flips lipids across the bilayer from the inner leaflet to the outward-open pocket before exporting them.
source: However, it is also possible that MlaFEDB flips lipids across the bilayer from the inner leaflet to the outward-open pocket observed in our structure before exporting them.
